rows.question: 1(a)
rows.answer: 23 kHz is above the usual human upper hearing limit of 20 kHz.
rows.learning: Convert kHz to Hz and compare with the boundaries of human hearing.

card.title: Above human hearing
card.prompt: Which frequency is ultrasonic?
card.modelAnswer: 28 kHz = 28,000 Hz, so it is ultrasound.
card.explanation: Ultrasound is sound above 20,000 Hz. A prefix can change a frequency by a factor of a thousand.
card.hint: What does kilo mean?
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: A sound does not become ultrasound simply because it is loud.

rows.question: 1(b)(i)
rows.answer: The repeller frequency lies in the mouse hearing range but above the human hearing range.
rows.learning: Explain an effect by comparing a frequency with the hearing ranges of different species.

card.title: Different ears, different ranges
card.prompt: A bat detects a 45 kHz sound but a person cannot. Explain why.
card.modelAnswer: 45 kHz is above the human upper hearing limit of about 20 kHz, but it is within the bat’s hearing range.
card.explanation: Hearing depends on whether the ear can respond to that frequency, not whether sound energy reaches it.
card.hint: Compare the same frequency with both animals’ ranges.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Do not say ultrasound cannot travel through air.

rows.question: 1(b)(ii)
rows.answer: Measure the wall distance and echo time, then divide twice the wall distance by the return time.
rows.learning: Plan a pulse-echo measurement and account for the outward and return journeys.

card.title: Measure sound with an echo
card.prompt: Describe how to find sound speed using an electronic pulse timer and a flat wall.

rubric.point: Time pulse emission to echo reception
Use twice the distance divided by time

card.modelAnswer: Measure the distance d from the device to the wall. Time a pulse from emission to reception of its echo. Calculate speed = 2d/t.
card.explanation: The timer measures a round trip. Counting only the outward distance would halve the calculated speed.
card.hint: Draw the two parts of the pulse’s journey.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: The echo time is not the one-way travel time.

rows.question: 2(a)
rows.answer: The spatial separation of equivalent wave points gives 28 cm.
rows.learning: Read wavelength from a distance axis, using two crests or two troughs.

card.title: Read a wavelength
card.prompt: Two neighbouring crests on a distance graph are at 0.12 m and 0.46 m. What is the wavelength?
card.explanation: One full cycle spans the distance between matching points on successive waves.
card.hint: Subtract the two crest positions.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: The height of a crest is amplitude, not wavelength.

rows.question: 2(b)(i)
rows.answer: Count complete waves passing a fixed point in a measured time, then use frequency = count/time.
rows.learning: Design a frequency measurement with a stopwatch and repeated oscillations.

card.title: Count the cycles
card.prompt: Describe a reliable way to measure the frequency of a floating marker bobbing on waves.

rubric.point: Measure the elapsed time for those cycles
Divide cycle count by elapsed time

card.modelAnswer: Count 20 complete oscillations and measure the elapsed time for those oscillations with a stopwatch. Frequency is the number of oscillations divided by the measured time in seconds. Repeat and average.
card.explanation: Timing many cycles makes the effect of reaction time smaller than timing just one cycle.
card.hint: Frequency means cycles per second.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Do not divide the time by the number; that gives period.

rows.question: 2(b)(ii)
rows.answer: λ = 1.5/0.70 = 2.14 m, approximately 2.1 m.
rows.learning: Rearrange v = fλ to find wavelength.

card.title: Use the wave equation
card.prompt: A wave travels at 2.4 m/s with frequency 0.80 Hz. Find its wavelength.
card.explanation: At a fixed speed, a lower frequency means each complete wave must be longer.
card.hint: Start from v = fλ.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: Multiplying speed by frequency gives the wrong units.

variants.prompt: A ripple travels at 3.6 m/s with frequency 0.90 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
A wave travels at 2.0 m/s with frequency 1.0 Hz. Find its wavelength.

rows.question: 2(b)(iii)
rows.answer: Transverse vibrations are perpendicular to travel; longitudinal vibrations are parallel to travel.
rows.learning: Define wave type using the direction of oscillation relative to energy transfer.

card.title: Two kinds of wave
card.prompt: Compare the vibration directions in transverse and longitudinal waves.
card.modelAnswer: In a transverse wave, particles vibrate perpendicular to wave travel. In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate parallel to wave travel.
card.explanation: The wave carries energy along while the medium’s particles oscillate about their normal positions.
card.hint: Use relative directions, not just up and down.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: A wave can travel horizontally while particles move vertically.

rows.question: 3(a)
rows.answer: All three emissions ionise matter and originate from unstable nuclei.
rows.learning: Recognise the shared properties of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.

card.title: What radioactive emissions share
card.prompt: Which property applies to alpha, beta and gamma emissions?
options: All come from unstable nuclei and can ionise matter
card.modelAnswer: They are emitted by unstable nuclei and can ionise atoms.
card.explanation: Ionisation means removing an electron from an atom. Neutral gamma photons can still cause ionisation.
card.hint: Think about origin and effect, not charge.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: Neutral radiation is not the same as harmless radiation.

rows.question: 3(b)
rows.answer: The nuclei contain the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
rows.learning: Explain isotope identity using proton number and neutron number.

card.title: Isotope identity
card.prompt: Compare the nuclei of oxygen-16 and oxygen-18.
card.modelAnswer: Both have 8 protons, so both are oxygen. Oxygen-16 has 8 neutrons and oxygen-18 has 10 neutrons.
card.explanation: An element is identified by proton number. Changing the number of neutrons changes its isotope.
card.hint: Mass number counts protons plus neutrons.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Isotopes do not have different numbers of protons.

rows.question: 3(c)(i)
rows.answer: Removing aluminium removes an absorber, so more beta particles reach the detector.
rows.learning: Link absorber penetration to a change in detected count.

card.title: Remove the shield
card.prompt: A thin aluminium sheet is removed from between a beta source and a detector. Explain why the count rises.

rubric.point: More particles reach detector after removal

card.modelAnswer: Aluminium absorbs some beta particles. Once the sheet is removed, more beta particles reach the detector each second.
card.explanation: A detector records the emissions that reach it; an absorber changes the measured count without changing nuclear decay.
card.hint: Distinguish emission rate from detected count rate.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Removing shielding does not make the source decay faster.

rows.question: 3(c)(ii)
rows.answer: Background radiation still reaches the detector when the source is removed.
rows.learning: Recognise and correct for environmental radiation in measurements.

card.title: A detector never quite reads zero
card.prompt: Why can a Geiger counter still register counts after the test source is taken away?
options: The removed source keeps producing echoes
All nearby air is highly radioactive
card.modelAnswer: Natural and artificial background radiation can still reach the detector.
card.explanation: Cosmic rays, rocks and building materials can contribute. Measure the background separately before measuring a weak source.
card.hint: Think about radiation from the surroundings.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: A nonzero reading does not prove the test source is still nearby.

rows.question: 3(c)(iii)
rows.answer: Activity is measured in becquerels, Bq; one Bq means one decay per second.
rows.learning: Distinguish activity from count totals and radiation dose.

card.title: Activity units
card.prompt: Which quantity is measured in becquerels?
options: Number of nuclear decays each second
Time for half the nuclei to decay
card.modelAnswer: Activity is the number of decays per second.
card.explanation: A source can have a high activity even when shielding means a nearby detector measures a small count rate.
card.hint: The unit is equivalent to one event per second.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: Becquerels are not a measure of absorbed dose.

rows.question: 3(d)
rows.answer: 33/11 = 3 half-lives; 1.7 × 10²³ / 8 = 2.125 × 10²² nuclei remain.
rows.learning: Use repeated halving and standard form for remaining undecayed nuclei.

card.title: Repeated half-lives
card.prompt: A sample starts with 6.4 × 10¹² unstable nuclei. Its half-life is 5 days. How many undecayed nuclei remain after 15 days?
card.modelAnswer: 15/5 = 3 half-lives. N = 6.4 × 10¹² / 2³ = 8.0 × 10¹¹ nuclei.
card.explanation: Half-life describes a fraction of the current amount, so three half-lives leave one eighth.
card.hint: First find the number of half-lives.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: Three half-lives do not leave one third of the sample.

rows.question: 4(a)
rows.answer: Cosmic microwave background radiation is evidence of the Universe’s hot, dense early state.
rows.learning: Distinguish evidence for an early hot Universe from evidence for expansion alone.

card.title: Evidence of the early Universe
card.prompt: Which observation most directly supports a hot, dense beginning to the Universe?
options: Microwave background radiation across the sky
card.modelAnswer: Cosmic microwave background radiation is leftover radiation from the early hot Universe.
card.explanation: Expansion stretches this radiation to microwave wavelengths. Its existence helped distinguish Big Bang cosmology from Steady State.
card.hint: Look for a relic of an early hot state.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: The existence of other galaxies alone does not demonstrate a beginning.

rows.question: 4(b)
rows.answer: Galaxy spectral wavelengths are longer than equivalent laboratory wavelengths, indicating recession and expansion.
rows.learning: Explain redshift as increased observed wavelength and connect it to recession.

card.title: Read the redshift
card.prompt: Light from a distant galaxy contains familiar spectral lines at longer wavelengths. Explain what this indicates.
card.modelAnswer: The spectral lines are redshifted: their wavelengths are increased. This indicates the galaxy is receding and supports an expanding Universe.
card.explanation: Comparing the same atomic lines lets us separate source motion from the line’s normal wavelength.
card.hint: Compare the observed line with its laboratory wavelength.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Redshift is not caused simply by red stars being present.

rows.question: 4(c)
rows.answer: Both theories allow expansion; Steady State has no beginning and requires continuous matter creation, unlike Big Bang.
rows.learning: Compare scientific models using a shared prediction and a discriminating difference.

card.title: Compare cosmological models
card.prompt: Give one similarity and one difference between the Big Bang and Steady State models.

rubric.point: Steady State has no beginning or creates matter continuously

card.modelAnswer: Both describe an expanding Universe. The Big Bang model has an early hot, dense state, whereas Steady State proposes an eternal Universe with continual matter creation.
card.explanation: Scientific models may share one successful prediction but differ on others; that is why additional observations matter.
card.hint: One shared prediction, then one real difference.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Do not say Steady State requires a static Universe.

rows.question: 4(d)(i)
rows.answer: The fitted line predicts approximately 1050 km/s at 15 Mpc.
rows.learning: Interpolate from a best-fit line rather than choosing an unrelated data point.

card.title: Read a galaxy trend
card.prompt: A best-fit recession-speed line passes through (0 Mpc, 0 km/s) and (20 Mpc, 1200 km/s). What speed does it predict at 12 Mpc?
card.modelAnswer: Gradient = 1200/20 = 60 km/s/Mpc. At 12 Mpc, v = 60 × 12 = 720 km/s.
card.explanation: Use the trend line for an estimate. Individual measurements may scatter around it.
card.hint: Find the speed gained for each Mpc.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: Read the line at the requested distance, not the nearest plotted measurement.

rows.question: 4(d)(ii)
rows.answer: The gradient is about 70 km/s/Mpc, calculated as velocity change divided by distance change.
rows.learning: Calculate a graph gradient and derive its compound units.

card.title: A gradient with units
card.prompt: A velocity-distance line rises from 300 km/s at 4 Mpc to 1500 km/s at 24 Mpc. Find its gradient.
card.explanation: A gradient is a change in the vertical quantity divided by a change in the horizontal quantity.
card.hint: Use two widely separated points on the line.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: Do not divide one point’s coordinates unless the line passes through the origin.

rows.question: 4(d)(iii)
rows.answer: Scatter permits several plausible best-fit lines and hence a range of gradients and age estimates.
rows.learning: Explain how data scatter creates uncertainty in a derived quantity.

card.title: Why a graph gives an estimate
card.prompt: A galaxy graph has widely scattered points. Explain why an age calculated from its gradient is uncertain.

rubric.point: Different gradients give different age estimates

card.modelAnswer: The scattered points allow several reasonable best-fit lines. Those lines have different gradients, so a calculation using the gradient gives a range of possible ages.
card.explanation: A calculated result cannot be more certain than the measurements and fitted line on which it depends.
card.hint: What happens if a different reasonable line is drawn?
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: A tidy calculation does not remove uncertainty from the data.

rows.question: 5(a)(i)
rows.answer: Draw a smooth curve through the origin and following the plotted refraction data.
rows.learning: Choose a smooth best-fit curve rather than joining experimental points with straight segments.

card.title: Fit the refraction results
card.prompt: Refraction data follow a smooth flattening trend. How should the best-fit graph be drawn?
options: Join every point with sharp straight segments
Draw a smooth curve following the trend
Ignore all points and draw a horizontal line
Force a straight line through the last two points
card.modelAnswer: Draw a smooth best-fit curve through the trend, including the origin when physically justified.
card.explanation: The shape represents the relationship, while small deviations may be measurement error.
card.hint: Choose the overall relationship rather than dot-to-dot.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: A best-fit curve does not have to hit every experimental point exactly.

rows.question: 5(a)(ii)
rows.answer: At incidence 80°, the fitted refracted angle is about 42° (accepted within 2°).
rows.learning: Use a curve to estimate an unmeasured refraction angle.

card.title: Estimate between measurements
card.prompt: For a refraction experiment, the smooth fitted curve gives r = 30° at i = 50° and r = 36° at i = 70°. Estimate r at i = 60° using linear interpolation between these nearby points.
card.modelAnswer: 60° is halfway from 50° to 70°, so r ≈ (30 + 36)/2 = 33°.
card.explanation: Interpolation estimates values between nearby measurements; the exact physical curve may be slightly curved.
card.hint: The requested incidence angle is halfway between the two given values.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: An interpolated estimate should not be presented as exact.

rows.question: 5(a)(iii)
rows.answer: The refracted angle increases with incidence angle, but its increase becomes smaller: the relationship is not proportional.
rows.learning: Describe both direction and shape of a graph trend.

card.title: Describe a curve properly
card.prompt: In a glass experiment, equal increases in incidence angle produce progressively smaller increases in refraction angle. Describe the relationship.
card.modelAnswer: The refraction angle increases as incidence angle increases, but at a decreasing rate. The relationship is not directly proportional.
card.explanation: A proportional relationship has constant gradient and passes through the origin; a flattening curve does not.
card.hint: State which way the values move and whether the rate changes.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Positive correlation does not automatically mean direct proportion.

rows.question: 5(b)
rows.answer: Entering glass reduces speed and wavelength, while frequency stays unchanged.
rows.learning: Use v = fλ when frequency is fixed at a boundary.

card.title: Light entering glass
card.prompt: A ray enters glass from air. Its frequency stays constant. Which pair changes correctly?
card.modelAnswer: Both speed and wavelength decrease in glass.
card.explanation: The source fixes frequency. With v = fλ and fixed f, a smaller wave speed requires a shorter wavelength.
card.hint: Keep frequency fixed in v = fλ.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: The light’s frequency does not decrease just because it slows down.

rows.question: 5(c)
rows.answer: Some light reflects at the air-glass boundary and some energy is absorbed in the glass, reducing transmitted intensity.
rows.learning: Explain a weaker transmitted beam through reflection and absorption.

card.title: Why the beam gets dimmer
card.prompt: A beam passes through a clear plastic block and emerges dimmer. Explain two ways its intensity can be reduced.

rubric.point: Less energy carried by transmitted beam

card.modelAnswer: Some light is reflected at the block’s surfaces and some is absorbed inside the plastic. Less energy per second remains in the transmitted beam, so it is dimmer.
card.explanation: Intensity measures energy transfer per unit area per second. Reflection redirects energy; absorption transfers it to the material.
card.hint: Consider what happens at a boundary and inside the material.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Refraction changes direction; it is not itself the same process as absorption.

rows.question: 5(d)
rows.answer: The correct graph shows constant lower speed inside glass and the original speed restored in air afterwards.
rows.learning: Interpret a piecewise graph for light moving through air, glass and air.

card.title: Speed through a block
card.prompt: How does light speed change along an air → glass → air path?
options: It falls continuously all the way
It drops on entering glass, stays steady there, then returns to its air value
It becomes greatest in the glass
card.modelAnswer: Speed is lower and constant in uniform glass, then returns to the air value on leaving.
card.explanation: Within each uniform material the speed is constant; a change occurs at its boundary.
card.hint: Ask which material the ray is in at each stage.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: Light is not permanently slowed after leaving the glass.

rows.question: 6(a)
rows.answer: Graph C is a straight displacement-time line with gradient 2 m/s.
rows.learning: Identify constant velocity from a displacement-time graph’s gradient.

card.title: Constant velocity on a graph
card.prompt: Which description represents steady motion at 3 m/s?
options: A displacement-time line rising 15 m in 5 s
A velocity-time line rising from 0 to 3 m/s
A displacement-time horizontal line at 3 m
A velocity-time line falling at 3 m/s each second
card.modelAnswer: A straight displacement-time line with gradient 15/5 = 3 m/s.
card.explanation: Velocity is the gradient of a displacement-time graph. A horizontal velocity-time line would also show constant velocity.
card.hint: Match the meaning of the graph’s axes.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: A rising velocity-time line means acceleration, not constant velocity.

rows.question: 6(b)(i)
rows.answer: a = (26 − 14)/34 = 0.3529… ≈ 0.35 m/s² to two significant figures.
rows.learning: Find acceleration from a velocity-time gradient and round appropriately.

card.title: Acceleration from two speeds
card.prompt: A tram’s speed rises steadily from 8 m/s to 20 m/s in 30 s. Calculate its acceleration.
card.explanation: Acceleration measures the change in velocity per second, so subtract the starting velocity first.
card.hint: Use the change in speed, not the final speed alone.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: 20/30 ignores the tram’s initial velocity.

variants.prompt: A train speeds up uniformly from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 8.0 s. Calculate its acceleration.
A tram speeds up from 10 m/s to 18 m/s in 10 s. Calculate its acceleration.

rows.question: 6(b)(ii)
rows.learning: Use the area of a trapezium under a velocity-time line for displacement.

card.title: Area under a velocity graph
card.prompt: A vehicle accelerates uniformly from 6 m/s to 18 m/s over 10 s. How far does it travel?
card.modelAnswer: Average velocity = (6 + 18)/2 = 12 m/s. Distance = 12 × 10 = 120 m.
card.explanation: The area under a velocity-time graph is displacement. For positive velocities and uniform acceleration, use the trapezium area.
card.hint: The average of the start and end speeds is useful here.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: Using only the triangular area forgets the initial-speed rectangle.

variants.prompt: A cart accelerates uniformly from 5 m/s to 10 m/s for 10 s. Calculate the distance travelled.
A vehicle accelerates uniformly from 2 m/s to 14 m/s in 8.0 s. How far does it travel?

rows.question: 6(c)
rows.answer: Burning fuel reduces rocket mass; at constant thrust its acceleration increases because a = F/m.
rows.learning: Use Newton’s second law to explain motion when mass changes.

card.title: A lighter rocket
card.prompt: A rocket burns fuel while its resultant driving force stays constant. Explain how its acceleration changes.
card.modelAnswer: Fuel is used up, so the rocket’s mass decreases. Since a = F/m, the same resultant force acts on a smaller mass and the acceleration increases.
card.explanation: The force needed for each unit of acceleration depends on how much mass is being accelerated.
card.hint: Rearrange F = ma.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Constant force does not guarantee constant acceleration if mass changes.

rows.question: 7(a)
rows.learning: Take the square root after substituting into a free-fall equation.

card.title: Time to fall
card.prompt: A ball is dropped from rest through 1.8 m. Use g = 10 m/s² and t² = 2h/g to find its fall time.
card.explanation: The equation gives time squared. Taking the positive square root gives the physical elapsed time.
card.hint: Your first calculation gives t², not t.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: 0.36 s is not the final time.

variants.prompt: A ball falls from rest through 0.80 m. Use g = 10 m/s² and t² = 2h/g to calculate its fall time.
A ball is dropped through 3.2 m. Neglect air resistance and use g = 10 m/s². Calculate the time from t² = 2h/g.

rows.question: 7(b)(i)
rows.answer: Human reaction delay is significant compared with the short measured fall time.
rows.learning: Recognise human timing error in short-duration experiments.

card.title: Timing a short fall
card.prompt: Why is a handheld stopwatch a poor choice for timing a 0.4 s fall?
options: Gravity stops acting before the timer starts
Reaction time is a large fraction of the measured time
The ball falls at constant speed
card.modelAnswer: Starting and stopping reaction delays are large compared with 0.4 s.
card.explanation: A delay that is unimportant over a minute can dominate a measurement lasting less than a second.
card.hint: Compare reaction delay with the event’s duration.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: Repeated readings reduce scatter but do not remove a consistent timing bias.

rows.question: 7(b)(ii)
rows.answer: Use light gates or another automatic timer to reduce reaction-time error.
rows.learning: Improve measurement validity by removing the dominant source of timing error.

card.title: Improve the timing
card.prompt: Which change best reduces reaction-time error when measuring a falling object’s travel time?
options: Ask the same person to press harder
Round the time to a whole second
card.modelAnswer: Light gates trigger electronically when the object passes, removing human button-press reaction delays.
card.explanation: An improvement should address the actual error, not merely repeat the same flawed procedure.
card.hint: What can start and stop the timer without a person?
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: Averaging does not automatically eliminate systematic error.

rows.question: 7(c)(i)
rows.answer: Average force magnitude = 8.7/0.35 = 24.86… ≈ 25 N.
rows.learning: Use force as momentum change per unit time.

card.title: Stopping force
card.prompt: A padded package loses 12 kg m/s of momentum while stopping in 0.40 s. Find the magnitude of the average resultant stopping force.
card.explanation: The same momentum change spread over more time needs a smaller average force.
card.hint: Use the momentum change divided by the stopping time.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: Do not multiply momentum by time.

rows.question: 7(c)(ii)
rows.answer: The box exerts a downward force of about 25 N on the floor, equal and opposite to the floor’s force on the box.
rows.learning: Identify equal-and-opposite interaction forces acting on different objects.

card.title: Action and reaction
card.prompt: A hand pushes a trolley east with 18 N. State the trolley’s force on the hand.
card.modelAnswer: The trolley pushes the hand west with 18 N.
card.explanation: Newton’s third law pairs forces from one interaction. They act on different bodies and therefore do not cancel on a single body.
card.hint: Swap which object exerts the force.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: The reaction force acts on the hand, not on the trolley.

rows.question: 7(d)
rows.learning: Link an energy or kinematics calculation to momentum.

card.title: Two equations, one answer
card.prompt: An object falls from rest through 5.0 m. Its momentum just before impact is 2.0 kg m/s. With g = 10 m/s² and negligible air resistance, calculate its mass.
card.explanation: The fall determines velocity independently of mass. Momentum then links that velocity to the unknown mass.
card.hint: Find the impact speed before using p = mv.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: Do not substitute height directly as a velocity.

rows.question: 8(a)
rows.answer: The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
rows.learning: Know the large-scale order of objects in the Solar System.

card.title: The asteroid belt
card.prompt: Where is the main asteroid belt?
card.modelAnswer: It lies mainly between Mars and Jupiter.
card.explanation: The main belt contains many small rocky bodies orbiting the Sun. It is different from the icy Kuiper belt beyond Neptune.
card.hint: Recall the order Earth, Mars, Jupiter.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: The asteroid belt is not the same as the Kuiper belt.

rows.question: 8(b)
rows.learning: Calculate orbital period from path length and orbital speed in standard form.

card.title: Time for an orbit
card.prompt: A small body travels 9.0 × 10¹¹ m in one orbit at a steady speed of 1.5 × 10⁴ m/s. Calculate its orbital period.
card.modelAnswer: T = distance/speed = (9.0 × 10¹¹)/(1.5 × 10⁴) = 6.0 × 10⁷ s.
card.explanation: Use the full orbital path length. Standard-form powers divide by subtracting their exponents.
card.hint: Distance divided by speed gives time.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: Orbital radius and distance travelled in one orbit are different quantities.

rows.question: 8(c)
rows.answer: The orbital velocity changes direction, so the asteroid accelerates even at constant speed.
rows.learning: Distinguish scalar speed from vector velocity in circular motion.

card.title: Constant speed can accelerate
card.prompt: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at steady speed. Explain why it is accelerating.
card.modelAnswer: The satellite’s velocity continuously changes direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so the satellite has an acceleration towards the centre even while its speed stays constant.
card.explanation: Acceleration is not restricted to speeding up or slowing down. A change of direction counts too.
card.hint: What extra information does velocity have compared with speed?
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Constant speed does not mean constant velocity.

rows.question: 8(d)
rows.answer: Vesta emits radiation at the same average rate as it absorbs solar energy, so its temperature can remain steady.
rows.learning: Explain equilibrium as equal incoming and outgoing power, not absence of energy transfer.

card.title: A planet’s steady temperature
card.prompt: A small planet absorbs sunlight continuously but its average temperature stays steady. Explain.

rubric.point: No net energy gain / constant temperature

card.modelAnswer: The planet emits thermal radiation. At equilibrium its emitted power equals its absorbed power, so there is no net increase in its internal energy and its average temperature remains steady.
card.explanation: Equilibrium is dynamic: energy still enters and leaves, but the amounts per second balance.
card.hint: Compare energy transferred each second in both directions.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: A steady temperature does not mean the planet has stopped absorbing sunlight.

rows.question: 8(e)(i)
rows.answer: The scheme identifies K with units W, equivalent to J/s.
rows.learning: Derive the units of a constant by rearranging an equation and combining units.

card.title: Units of a constant
card.prompt: Radiation intensity I is in W/m² and I = K/r², with r measured in metres. What is the unit of K?
card.modelAnswer: K = Ir², so (W/m²) × m² = W.
card.explanation: Units follow the same multiplication and division rules as algebra. Squaring a length also squares its unit.
card.hint: Rearrange to K = Ir².
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: W and W/s are not interchangeable.

rows.question: 8(e)(ii)
rows.answer: Intensity = 1400/(2.4²) = 243 W/m², approximately 240 W/m².
rows.learning: Use an inverse-square relationship to compare intensity at different distances.

card.title: Further from a source
card.prompt: A star’s intensity is 1800 W/m² at distance r. What is its intensity at distance 3r?
card.explanation: The same power is spread over a spherical area proportional to radius squared. Tripling distance spreads it over nine times the area.
card.hint: Square the distance multiplier.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: Tripling distance does not merely divide intensity by three.

variants.prompt: A star’s intensity at distance r is 900 W/m². What is it at 3r?
A star’s intensity at distance r is 3200 W/m². Calculate its intensity at 4r.

rows.question: 9(a)
rows.answer: Radioactive material enters the body and can irradiate nearby cells from within, causing damage or cancer.
rows.learning: Explain why contamination differs from external irradiation.

card.title: Contamination inside the body
card.prompt: Explain why swallowing a small amount of an alpha-emitting material can be dangerous.

rubric.point: Radioactive material remains inside and emits radiation

card.modelAnswer: The radioactive material is inside the body and emits alpha particles close to living cells. Their strong ionisation can damage cells and DNA, increasing cancer risk.
card.explanation: Alpha radiation is easily stopped by skin but is highly ionising over its short range inside tissue.
card.hint: Think about what happens when the skin barrier is bypassed.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Low external penetration does not make internal contamination safe.

rows.question: 9(b)
rows.answer: Penetrating gamma radiation kills microorganisms throughout food and helps preserve it.
rows.learning: Connect a radiation property to a useful application.

card.title: Preserving packaged food
card.prompt: Why can gamma radiation be useful for treating sealed food packages?
card.modelAnswer: Gamma rays penetrate the package and food, killing microorganisms and reducing spoilage.
card.explanation: High penetration allows treatment through packaging. Irradiating food does not normally make the food radioactive.
card.hint: Link penetration to reaching microorganisms throughout the package.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Irradiation and radioactive contamination are different processes.

rows.question: 9(c)
rows.answer: The nucleus loses energy and becomes more stable; proton and neutron numbers stay the same.
rows.learning: Recognise gamma emission as de-excitation rather than a change of nuclear composition.

card.title: Gamma emission
card.prompt: What happens to a nucleus when it emits a gamma photon?
options: It loses energy without changing proton or neutron number
Its mass number increases by four
card.modelAnswer: The nucleus moves to a lower energy state with unchanged proton and neutron numbers.
card.explanation: Gamma emission releases excess nuclear energy. It does not change the identity of the element.
card.hint: A gamma photon contains no protons or neutrons.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: Gamma emission is not alpha emission.

rows.question: 9(d)
rows.answer: Alpha emission releases a helium nucleus, reducing mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2. Beta-minus emission releases an electron as a neutron becomes a proton: mass number is unchanged and atomic number rises by 1.
rows.learning: Construct a linked comparison of radiation composition, charge and nuclear changes.

card.title: Compare two decays
card.prompt: Compare alpha decay with beta-minus decay. Include each emitted particle and changes to the parent nucleus.
card.modelAnswer: Alpha decay emits a positively charged helium nucleus containing two protons and two neutrons, so the parent’s mass number falls by 4 and atomic number falls by 2. Beta-minus decay emits an electron when a neutron converts into a proton; mass number stays the same and atomic number rises by 1.
card.explanation: Count the nucleons before and after. Alpha physically removes four nucleons; beta-minus changes the type of one nucleon but not the total number.
card.hint: Organise your answer as alpha: particle and changes; beta-minus: particle and changes.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: The beta electron is created in the nuclear process; it is not an ordinary orbital electron leaving the atom.

rows.question: 10(a)(i)
rows.answer: Examples include solar, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal and biomass energy.
rows.learning: Identify energy resources replenished on a human timescale.

card.title: Renewable resources
card.prompt: Which pair contains only renewable energy resources?
card.modelAnswer: Geothermal and tidal resources are renewable.
card.explanation: Renewable means naturally replenished; it does not mean there are no environmental effects.
card.hint: Check both resources in each pair.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: Nuclear fuel is low-carbon in use but is not renewable.

rows.question: 10(a)(ii)
rows.answer: Efficiency = 2.2/6.2 = 0.355, or about 35%.
rows.learning: Calculate useful output divided by total input and distinguish fraction from percentage.

card.title: Useful output
card.prompt: A generator receives 8.0 kJ each second and supplies 3.2 kJ each second usefully. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.
card.modelAnswer: Efficiency = useful output/total input × 100 = 3.2/8.0 × 100 = 40%.
card.explanation: An efficiency of 40% means 40 of every 100 units of input energy become useful output.
card.hint: The useful output belongs on top of the fraction.
steps: Write the relevant equation.
Substitute the values using consistent units.
Calculate, round sensibly and give the unit.
card.misconception: Do not report the fraction 0.40 with a percent sign.

variants.prompt: A generator receives 12.5 kJ and transfers 7.5 kJ usefully. Calculate percentage efficiency.
A turbine receives 20 kJ and gives 9.0 kJ of useful output. Calculate its percentage efficiency.

rows.question: 10(a)(iii)
rows.answer: Some energy remains in moving air or is dissipated by friction; not all input energy becomes useful electrical output.
rows.learning: Explain practical limits on useful energy conversion without claiming energy disappears.

card.title: Where unused energy goes
card.prompt: Why can a real turbine not convert all incoming wind energy into useful electrical output?
options: Some energy is dissipated by friction and some remains in moving air
Energy is destroyed by the blades
The generator creates extra input energy
card.modelAnswer: Some energy is transferred to thermal stores by friction and the air still carries kinetic energy after passing the blades.
card.explanation: Energy is conserved. Efficiency describes the share transferred usefully, not the share that continues to exist.
card.hint: Follow both the air and the moving machinery.
steps: Read the physical situation.
Rule out alternatives using the stated physics.
Choose the statement that fits all the evidence.
card.misconception: Wasted energy is not destroyed energy.

rows.question: 10(b)
rows.answer: Fission splits a heavy nucleus after neutron absorption and can sustain a chain reaction, but produces long-lived radioactive waste. Fusion joins light nuclei at extreme temperature and pressure; sustaining controlled practical power generation is difficult.
rows.learning: Compare nuclear mechanisms with practical benefits and challenges, using linked scientific reasoning.

card.title: Fission or fusion for power?
card.prompt: Compare fission and fusion as possible electricity sources. Explain both processes and one practical difficulty for each.
card.modelAnswer: Fission splits a heavy nucleus after neutron absorption, releasing energy and more neutrons that can sustain a chain reaction. Fission produces radioactive waste needing long-term management. Fusion joins light nuclei and releases energy. Fusion requires extremely high temperatures and difficult plasma confinement, making sustained practical power generation challenging.
card.explanation: Both release nuclear energy, but their engineering problems differ. Avoid claiming fusion has no radiation issues: some designs produce neutrons that can activate materials.
card.hint: Compare process, energy release and engineering challenge for each.
steps: Identify the physical idea.
Link each statement to a reason or observation.
Check that every part of the question is answered.
card.misconception: Fusion does not mean burning hydrogen chemically.
